source: Mahbub and Feng (2025/2026, AAAI) Mitigating Self-Preference by Authorship Obfuscation
finding: Judges recognise their own answers from word choice. Changing two words in the answer lowers self-recognition and lowers harmful self-preference. Rewriting the rival answer in the judge's own style backfires and raises self-preference, because the judge then picks the answer it agrees with.
numbers: QuALITY long-document QA, 2,086 validation items, 5 judges (Llama-3.1-8B to DeepSeek-V3). Two-word synonym swap: paired t-test p<.01 on judge accuracy in cases where the judge's own answer is wrong. Extra judges, accuracy when own answer is wrong, original to swapped: Mistral-Small-24B 26.78 to 33.52 percent, Kimi-K2 28.84 to 32.18, GPT-OSS-20B 28.28 to 31.43, GLM-4.5-Air 60.56 to 63.94. Self-recognition fell by about 1.1 to 3.3 points on those four. Human check: 30 annotators, 500 examples, original and swapped judged equal quality.
quote: perturbations as simple as synonym replacement for a few words predictably reduce self-preference
limits: Answers to multiple-choice questions with a known truth, not ideas. Gains are a few points, not removal. Full style neutralisation makes it worse. Self-preference partly tracks what the judge believes is correct.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. Masking source cues helps a little; a different-model judge is still needed because belief agreement survives masking. Never rewrite candidates into the judge's own voice before judging.

source: Chae et al. (2026) Self- and Other-Labels Induce Bidirectional Bias in LLM Judges (blind evaluation, Experiment 1)
finding: With the text style removed from the task, apparent self-preference mostly comes from selection quality and two lenient judges, not from judges favouring themselves. Raw self-minus-other gaps go both ways across ten judges.
numbers: 10 LLM judges (Kimi K2.6, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok 4.3 and others) scored narrative-constraint selections on a 4-part rubric. Raw self minus other: Kimi +1.09, GPT-5.5 +0.86, Opus 4.7 +0.51, Mistral Large 3 -0.08, Grok 4.3 -0.67, Qwen3.6-35B -0.90 (Holm-corrected Welch tests; significant for 5). Mixed-effects self-preference coefficient on the average score: +0.181 [0.13, 0.23] with all 10 judges, +0.003 [-0.05, 0.06] after dropping 2 low-discrimination judges. Originality coefficient stayed negative, -0.133 [-0.21, -0.05].
quote: self-preference disappears, with a small effect remaining in the opposite direction
limits: Judges rate sets of narrative constraints, not whole ideas or prose. The exclusion of two judges is a post-hoc step, though a random-slope refit on all ten also found no effect. Scale of scores not stated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. Self-preference in judging selections is small once quality is controlled. This weakens K13 for idea picking but does not remove the label effect in the next line.

source: Chae et al. (2026) Self- and Other-Labels Induce Bidirectional Bias in LLM Judges (labelled evaluation, Experiment 2)
finding: Telling a judge that a selection was its own raises the score, and telling it the selection came from someone else lowers it, even when the content is identical. The true source has no effect.
numbers: Label main effect on the average score +0.43 [0.39, 0.47], p<.001. Per dimension: originality +0.53, dimensionality +0.57, coherence +0.29, tellability +0.32. True-source effect +0.02 [-0.09, 0.14], p=.689. Label by source interaction -0.01, p=.823. Self-labels raised scores by 0.29 to 0.57 in every actual-source block.
limits: Labels said only 'yours' or 'someone else's', no model name. Same ten judges and same narrative-constraint task as Experiment 1. Scale of the score not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. Hiding authorship is worth doing. Do not tell the judge call which candidates it wrote, and do not label candidates 'yours'. Effect is larger than any real source effect found here.

source: Domanti et al. (2026) The Effect of Idea Elaboration on the Automatic Assessment of Idea Originality
finding: Three automatic raters scored ChatGPT-4o's alternate-uses answers as more original than both human groups. Part of that was answer length and elaboration. When only the core idea was scored, ChatGPT-4o's answers dropped below the high-creative humans.
numbers: 4,813 alternate-uses responses from 81 psychology students (split by median into higher and lower creative) and ChatGPT-4o; raters OCSAI, CLAUS and ChatGPT-4o against two trained human raters. ChatGPT-4o as rater scored its own responses 3.49 on the full answer and 2.06 on the core idea (drop of 1.43). With core ideas, all three raters put high-creative humans above ChatGPT-4o, but OCSAI and CLAUS still put ChatGPT-4o above low-creative humans.
limits: Italian-language answers, one machine producer, a 1 to 5 originality scale. Core-idea extraction is itself a model step. Self-preference and elaboration are not fully separable here.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. The self-preference effect in idea scoring is partly a length and elaboration effect. A cheap code control is to compare ideas at equal length, or to score a one-line core idea.

source: Bansal et al. (2026) Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
finding: Frontier models predicting the score change of their own proposed ML ideas, before training, are clearly better than chance but explain at most half of the variance. They get the sign right most of the time and shrink the size of changes.
numbers: 288 ideas on 8 MLE-bench tasks, 269 analysed after 19 failed runs; 3 models proposed and implemented 12 ideas per task tree. R2: Claude Opus 5.5 0.49, Claude Fable 5.1 0.41, GPT-6 Astra 0.38, GLM-5.3 0.18, Kimi K3 0.13. Direction right: 82, 78, 76, 72, 69 percent. Under a Gaussian model the top-ranked idea would capture about 70 percent of the best gain for Opus 5.5, 64 for Fable 5.1, 62 for GPT-6, 42 for GLM, 36 for Kimi.
limits: Small tabular and text ML tasks with fast training. Ideas were prompted to improve or worsen the score, so half were meant to fail. Not research ideas in the Si sense. 2026 model names as printed by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. Execution outcome as ground truth: a 2026 frontier judge does beat chance by a wide margin when the idea is a concrete code change with a measurable score. A cheap small run (the actual check) is the ceiling this judge approximates.

source: Bansal et al. (2026), self-preference check, section 5.4
finding: Models did not rate their own ideas more optimistically than other models rated them. Which coding harness implemented the idea also had little effect.
numbers: Residual of a model's prediction on its own ideas minus residual of the other four models on the same idea: +0.01, 95 percent interval -0.06 to +0.08. All three diagonal cells at most +0.03.
limits: Numeric outcome prediction on ML tasks, not taste judgement on prose. Controls for idea quality by comparing models on the same idea.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. When the judge must predict a checkable number, self-preference is not visible. Argues for making the judge output a falsifiable prediction.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf frontier models are near chance at picking which of two research ideas will score higher. A GPT-4.1 fine-tuned on past outcomes with paper retrieval beats 25 human experts in NLP. This is a judge that beats the human ceiling.
numbers: 1,585 test pairs after cutoff, 6,000 training pairs. Zero-shot GPT-4.1 51.9 percent; o1 and o3 similar or slightly better. Fine-tuned system 77 percent on full test set; NLP subset 64.4 percent vs 48.9 percent for human expert majority; best-annotator ceiling 60.0 percent; human inter-annotator agreement 75.1 percent. On 33 unpublished idea pairs, executed by experts at about 103.4 hours per idea, 63.6 percent, including ideas from an AI ideation agent.
limits: Pairs where the ideas are very similar in kind (two jailbreak methods). 33 pairs is a tiny test. Needs a labelled outcome set for fine-tuning, which a scaffold-only agent does not have.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. Judge quality for unexecuted ideas only rose above the human ceiling through outcome-based training. A prompt-only judge stays near 50 to 60 percent. The scaffold should not depend on judge ranking without a run.

source: Mule et al. (2026) Teaching Language Models to Forecast Research Success Through Comparative Idea Evaluation
finding: Zero-shot 8B models score about 30 percent on a pairwise task and GPT-5 is only modestly above 50 percent on picking the better of two ideas. Training on outcomes lifts small models above GPT-5.
numbers: 11,488 idea pairs from PapersWithCode. Abstract: off-the-shelf 8B models about 30 percent, SFT 77.1 percent, GPT-5 61.1 percent, reasoning-trained (RLVR) 71.35 percent. Table 2 as extracted: GPT-5 57.65 default, 59.61 low thinking, 61.10 medium thinking; Gemini 2.5 Flash 40.73. Appending chain of thought to Llama 3.1 cut accuracy from 30.02 to 27.38.
limits: Table layout garbled in the text extract, so only the GPT-5 rows and abstract numbers are quoted. Accuracy well below 50 percent for base models suggests the metric counts unparsed or tied answers as wrong, so 'chance' here is not simply 50. Cause not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. A 2026 frontier model with more thinking gains about 3 to 4 points on idea pairing. Still far from reliable. Confirms that judge calls should be treated as weak votes.

source: Gong, Li and Zhou (2026) LLMs learn scientific taste from institutional traces across the social sciences
finding: Models fine-tuned on where research pitches were published beat 11 frontier reasoning models and expert gatekeepers on a 4-tier ranking of untested research pitches, with calibrated confidence.
numbers: Eight social science fields. Best single model accuracy from 55.0 percent (public administration) to 85.5 percent (psychology). Management: Qwen3-4B 59.2 percent vs expert majority vote 41.6 percent (48 gatekeepers) vs 31.1 percent mean of 11 frontier reasoning models; chance 25 percent; 174 junior researchers also compared.
limits: Read from the abstract page only (paraphrased fetch), not the PDF. Tier labels reflect journal prestige, not true quality. Training needed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. A judge that beats the human agreement ceiling exists only as a trained model. Prompt-only frontier models sat only 6 points above chance on a 4-way task.

source: Li (2026) The Ideation Bottleneck: Decomposing the Quality Gap Between AI-Generated and Human Economics Research
finding: Outside NLP prompting, in economics, the AI-versus-human gap is mostly an idea gap, not an execution gap. Idea quality and execution quality were nearly uncorrelated in AI papers.
numbers: 953 papers: 912 AI-generated (APE project) and 41 human papers from AER and AEJ:Policy. Idea quality d=2.23; human 47.1 percent mean 'exceptional' probability vs 16.5 percent for AI. Execution d=0.90; 4.38 vs 3.84 out of 5. Idea quality about 71 percent of the gap, execution 29 percent. 7 of 912 AI papers (0.8 percent) beat the median human paper on both.
limits: Both measures are model judgements: an idea tier model fine-tuned on management journals and one Gemini judge for execution. No human experts, no execution-to-outcome ground truth. Opposite direction of emphasis from Si 2025, so it is not a replication of the gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Does not replicate the 'ideas look good, fail at execution' finding. It finds the opposite bottleneck with a different judge. The ideation-execution split depends on field and method, so G8 must not assume one direction.

source: Si et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap (re-read for design limits)
finding: The execution study reused ideas from the earlier ideation study, assigned them at random to executors within chosen topics, and states its own limits. It does not discuss regression to the mean or selection of top-scored ideas.
numbers: N=43 executed projects, 7 NLP prompting topics, 58 expert reviewers, pre-registered at OSF. Searches of the text extract for 'regress', 'winner' and 'selection effect' found nothing relevant.
limits: Ideas were scoped to be feasible in three months and to novel prompting methods; the authors say this limits generalisation to modelling or training work. Whether the AI arm was drawn from the top-ranked set is not analysed as a source of the drop.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. The share of the gap due to regression after selection on a noisy score is unmeasured. Judge noise near 56 percent agreement makes some regression likely. Treat the gap as an upper bound on true judge-versus-outcome loss.

source: Zhang (2026) Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation
finding: Ranking raw ideas with a model judge and keeping the top did nothing. Revising ideas helped, and revising a diverse subset cost less than revising all. Selecting alone did not help; transforming did.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B as generator and judge, 10 seeds, 10 research-ideation environments, 50 candidates per seed. Raw first-n and rerank-only: 0 research-strong non-duplicate ideas. Refine all: 21.8 (115.4k tokens). Random-k (40 of 50): slightly more at 105.0k tokens. MMR-k: 23.70 vs 22.18, duplicate rate 0.172 vs 0.186. Blinded panel of 4 outside-family judges, 72 items, 1 to 9 composite: raw 5.34, rerank 5.29, refine all 7.01, random-k 6.91, MMR-k 6.77, micro-low 6.77.
limits: A 3B model, proxy rubric, no expert or execution check. Authors say the claims are limited to proxy-rated portfolios. Per-item ranking among refined methods varied by judge.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8. At matched generator, the judge-and-pick step alone gave no external-panel gain (5.34 to 5.29); a revision step did (about +1.5). Worth testing random-k versus judge-k before trusting the judge.

source: Ueda et al. (2025) Exploring Design of Multi-Agent LLM Dialogues for Research Ideation
finding: One agent generating and others critiquing and revising raises idea diversity over a single generator. Diversity rises with critique-revision turns up to three and with up to three parallel critics, then flattens.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, 7 topics x 10 configurations x 20 seeds x 5 ideas = 7,000 raw ideas; dedup at cosine 0.8. Non-duplicate ratio: single no-critique 0.69; self-critique 1 turn 0.77; 2 turns 0.80; 3 turns 0.85; 4 turns 0.86 (table values from extract). Best Precision@10 0.52 at 3 turns; fourth turn 'negligible gains and sometimes hurts precision'. 1 to 3 critics: 0.77 to 0.80. Specialist critic won 0.55 vs baseline at N=10; specialist proposer gave highest diversity 0.81.
limits: Quality judged by a GPT-4 pairwise tournament against the self-critique baseline, with no human check; Si 2024 found such judges near chance. Calls and tokens not matched across arms. Table text partly garbled in extract.
agent_relevance: Gap 8. Code-measurable stop rule exists: stop when the embedding non-duplicate ratio gains under about 0.01 per round (reached after round 3). Quality side still unproven.

source: Maryanskyy, Budnikov and Kaliyev (2026) When Agents Disagree: The Selection Bottleneck in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
finding: In generate-then-select pipelines, the selector matters more than generator diversity. Judge-based selection over a diverse team beat a single strong model; synthesising answers together did not.
numbers: 42 tasks in 7 categories, N=210 comparisons. Diverse team with judge selection win rate 0.810 vs a single-model baseline (Opus-only); homogeneous team 0.512 (Glass's delta 2.07). Synthesis preferred over baseline in 0 of 42 tasks by the judge panel (difference in win rate +0.631 for selection). With fully independent judges, rank order held (Spearman 0.90) but win rates shrank 53 to 67 percent.
limits: Judge panel and generator share model families in the primary cells, which the authors call partial circularity. General tasks, not ideation. Compares selection against synthesis, not separate-call against single-call generation.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. Indirect support for a separate selection step, with the caveat that more than half of the measured gain vanishes under independent judging.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Non-reasoning models correct an error when it is shown as coming from the user but not when it sits in their own output. Reasoning models do not show the gap. Appending 'Wait' closes most of it.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5 percent. Appending 'Wait': blind spot down 89.3 percent, mean accuracy up 156 percent. Fine-tuning with 5,306 correction traces: blind spot down 76.0 percent. Reasoning models: blind spot small or negative. Of errors a model misses in its own natural output, 4.3 to 10.8 percent are caught when the same error is shown externally. Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5 percent and Claude Sonnet 4 41.4 percent blind spot (Table 7); 62.8 percent average on non-math BIG-Bench Mistake tasks.
limits: Injected errors on math-style tasks (GSM8K-SC, PRM800K-SC), not open-ended ideas. Measures activation of correction, not net accuracy at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Models judge better when the text is framed as someone else's. Supports a judge call that presents candidates as external. Reasoning models self-check inside their thinking, so an extra critique call adds less for them.

source: Stav et al. (2026) When Does Intrinsic Self-Correction Help? A Task-Sensitive Analysis
finding: Intrinsic self-correction helps a lot on tasks with checkable structure (SAT constraints) and a little on hard reasoning, with some harm on others. In 2026 models the gains persist, smaller for the strongest model.
numbers: Five models (Mistral Large 2512, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek V3.1, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Gemini Pro). SAT accuracy base to self-correct: Mistral 34.62 to 64.96, Haiku 75.64 to 93.59, DeepSeek 78.63 to 92.74, Flash Lite 60.68 to 82.91, Gemini Pro 97.00 to 100. SAT removes on average 65.66 percent of baseline errors. Right-to-wrong flips up to 13.25 percent on BBEH and HLE vs at most 2.1 percent on SAT. BBEH sub-tasks range from +16.2 percent (Zebra puzzles) to -4.3 percent (movie recommendation).
limits: Matched tokens not controlled; self-correction uses extra calls. Whether the models used extended thinking is not stated in the text read. Not open-ended generation.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Huang 2024's null for self-critique is task-bound, not universal. A self-check pays when the check can be stated as explicit constraints; for open-ended ideas it does not yet have evidence.

source: Tie et al. (2025) Can LLMs Correct Themselves? A Benchmark of Self-Correction in LLMs (CorrectBench)
finding: Self-correction improves accuracy on commonsense, maths and code tasks, mixing methods helps more but costs more, and reasoning models gain only marginally at high time cost. A plain chain-of-thought baseline is competitive on accuracy and efficiency.
numbers: Three task types; instruction models (LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and reasoning models (DeepSeek-V3, R1 and o3-mini discussed). Statement in text: 'For reasoning LLMs, these methods offer only marginal gains with increased time usage.' Cost table on MATH uses 150 samples.
limits: Benchmark-level numbers were not extracted line by line. Mostly external or fine-tuned correction methods are included beside intrinsic ones. Covers 2024 to early 2025 models, not 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. Indirect answer: reasoning models see little added from a separate critique pass, so extra judge calls should be reserved for non-reasoning stages or for checks with an external signal.

source: He et al. (2025) Common and specific neural correlates underlying creative generation and evaluation: An ALE meta-analysis
finding: A coordinate meta-analysis finds partly separate networks for generation and evaluation. It does not show the medial temporal lobe for generation, which Ellamil reported.
numbers: 44 generation studies and 10 evaluation studies. Generation: superior and medial frontal gyri, cingulate, inferior frontal gyrus, inferior parietal lobe, precentral gyrus, middle frontal gyrus. Evaluation: insula, claustrum, inferior frontal gyrus, medial frontal gyrus, cingulate. Evaluation over generation: insula and claustrum cluster, and medial frontal plus cingulate cluster. Conjunction: inferior frontal gyrus common to both.
limits: Abstract only. Only 10 evaluation studies, so the evaluation map is thin. Studies differ in task and in how evaluation was elicited.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Gives a later pooled check of the Ellamil contrast: the split holds for insula-linked evaluation, but the MTL story for generation is not reproduced. The neural case for a split stays moderate, which fits keeping G5 as a design choice.

source: Pidgeon et al. (2016) Functional neuroimaging of visual creativity: a systematic review and meta-analysis (table entry for Ellamil et al. 2012)
finding: The review table gives the sample and design of Ellamil 2012: art and design students alternated between designing and evaluating book covers, against a line-tracing control.
numbers: 15 participants (9 female), mean age 22.14 (SD 2.25). Generate: design and sketch book covers from descriptions of documentaries. Evaluate: write or sketch evaluations of the covers made in the Generate stage. Control: trace lines. Generate over Evaluate: left inferior frontal gyrus, cerebellum, bilateral hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex, premotor, superior parietal. Evaluate over Generate: anterior and posterior cingulate, precuneus, left anterior insula, superior frontal (BA 10), middle and inferior frontal, temporopolar cortex and others.
limits: Secondary report, not the original paper; thresholds, phase durations and motion handling are not given. The original full text was not reachable (publisher paywall; the UBC thesis page blocked automated access). N=15 is small, and phases were in a fixed alternation with different motor output (sketching vs writing).
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Establishes N=15 and that the two phases differed in motor and language demand, so some of the contrast is not about generating versus judging. Thresholds and phase purity remain unconfirmed.

source: Hao et al. (2016) Reflection enhances creativity: Beneficial effects of idea evaluation on idea generation
finding: Pausing mid-task to mentally evaluate the ideas already produced made later ideas more original than pausing for a distraction task. Evaluation placed inside generation helped generation.
numbers: EEG study on the alternative uses task; a reflection task or a distraction task was inserted during generation. Originality higher after evaluation. Upper alpha (10 to 13 Hz) synchronisation was strongest at frontal sites and generation alpha rose after evaluation. Sample size not read.
limits: Abstract only, no N or effect size. Uses one task. The evaluation was mental, not a separate scored judgement.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5. A direct human test where interleaving evaluation improved generation: against a hard split. Suggests a short code-timed review step between generation bursts is worth testing against a pure two-call split.

source: Rietzschel, Nijstad and Stroebe (2010) The selection of creative ideas after individual idea generation: choosing between creativity and impact
finding: People choose feasible and desirable ideas over original ones, which is why generating more ideas does not produce better selected ideas. Rating each idea first, or being told to exclude ideas, did not help. Telling people to pick original ideas raised originality but lowered satisfaction and rated effectiveness.
numbers: Abstract gives no sample size or effect size. Cited by 340 works (Crossref).
limits: Abstract only. Human selectors, not language models. Primary papers for Jansson and Smith 1991 and the Sio 2015 meta-analysis on example fixation could not be opened (paywall), so gap 5 effect sizes stay unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 10. A selector with one blended preference drifts toward feasibility. Supports scoring novelty and feasibility separately with code-set weights, and an explicit 'pick the most original' instruction in the selection call.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench (re-opened for human baseline and regeneration result)
finding: The human reference is eight authors of the paper. Regeneration with earlier answers in context brought three frontier models to about human-writer diversity, and two of them above human cumulative utility.
numbers: NB-Curated: 100 prompts answered by 8 authors each, 8 generations per model. In-context regeneration: Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro roughly match human distinct counts (out of 8); GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceed human utility. Paraphrasing and a 'producer of unique answers' system prompt were only marginally effective. Authors call the eight-author group a lower bound on human diversity.
limits: Human baseline is eight homogeneous annotators, so the claim 'matches human level' is weak. Utility mixes distinctness with a reward-model quality score; no separate human quality rating of the added answers.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. Not answered: no larger human baseline has been found. Quality is only partly protected because utility includes a quality term. Keep the 'show prior outputs' trick, but measure quality with a held-out rater.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (Table 10 and section 6.3 re-opened)
finding: Reviewers' overall score tracks novelty and excitement and is unrelated to feasibility. So a single blended score hides one criterion.
numbers: Overall vs novelty r=0.725; overall vs excitement r=0.854; overall vs feasibility r=0.097; novelty vs feasibility r=-0.073; excitement vs feasibility r=-0.031; overall vs effectiveness r=0.642. Inter-reviewer agreement 56.1 percent vs NeurIPS 2021 66.0 percent and ICLR 2024 71.9 percent.
limits: Human reviewer correlations from the ideation study, not from LLM judges. No study found that compares a two-score judge with a blended judge against held-out raters, so gap 10 is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 10. Since novelty and feasibility are uncorrelated, a two-score judge with a code-set weight loses nothing and lets the agent set the trade-off. Direct comparison against held-out raters remains to be run.

source: Matheson et al. (2023) Representing creative thought: a representational similarity analysis of creative idea generation and evaluation
finding: Information from the generation phase is re-instated in later evaluation within both executive and default regions and between them. The two phases share representations, so they are not isolated systems.
numbers: Abstract: strong evidence for reinstatement within dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the novelty task and within medial prefrontal cortex in the appropriateness task; between-network reinstatement for dorsolateral prefrontal and posterior parietal in the novelty task. No N read.
limits: Abstract only. Word-association task.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Adds a second, different design pointing to coupling. A judge call must be given the generator's content in full; a judge working from a summary loses the shared representation.
